svg.title: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when something breaks it: init heals a revoked token, a tampered variable and a duplicate token, and reload puts a drifted project back
svg.text: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when something
Scenario: init heals a revoked token, a tampered variable and a duplicate token, and reload puts a drifted
A revoked release token is rebuilt
A duplicate token and a tampered variable are repaired
A project that drifted is put back in one command

g.text: Given a project the framework set up, whose release token someone then revoked in GitLab
GitLab's access-tokens page of a project after its first `task devsecops:init`. That run created two tokens, the release
token TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN and the dependency robot's TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN.
Someone has since revoked the release token in GitLab. "Active project access tokens" lists only TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN,
and the release token sits under "Inactive project access tokens", marked "Revoked". Dates, last use and expiry change
on every run, so they are blanked.
When the developer runs the framework's init again, a brand-new release token takes the
revoked one's place
The developer runs `task devsecops:init` again. "Active project access tokens" lists TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN once more: a
new token, while the old one stays below, still "Revoked".
The same run stored the new token in the CI/CD variable of the same name. The test checks that this variable, like the
dependency robot's, really clones the repository.
When the developer runs init a second time, GitLab keeps that release token and revokes
nothing
A second `task devsecops:init` on the healed project. The page has not changed: the same release token is active, and
"Inactive project access tokens" still holds one row. The init run found a working token and left it alone.
When someone plants a second release token with the same name in GitLab
The same project. Someone creates a second token named TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN in GitLab, so "Active project access
tokens" now lists two release tokens where there should be one.
And someone overwrites the release token's CI/CD variable with a bad value
Someone also overwrites the release token's CI/CD variable. The project's CI/CD settings, values shown with "Reveal
values": TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN now holds "tampered-by-e2e", which no pipeline can sign in with.
TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN still holds a real token. It starts with "glpat-" like every GitLab token, and its secret part is
masked as "*****".
When the developer runs the framework's init once more, a single release token is left
One more `task devsecops:init`. "Active project access tokens" lists a single release token again, and "Inactive project
access tokens" now holds three.
The first is the token revoked in chapter 1. The second is the older of the two duplicates, which the init run revoked.
The third is the one it kept, which it then replaced with a new token because the CI/CD variable no longer matched it.
Then the CI/CD variable holds a GitLab token again instead of the bad value
The same CI/CD settings page, values revealed. TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN holds a GitLab token again, "glpat-" with its
secret part masked, where it held "tampered-by-e2e". The test checks that this new value clones the repository.
Given a project the framework set up, whose main branch someone then loosened by hand
A new project, generated from the toolbox and set up on install day. Its repository settings, "Protected branches": the
main branch says "Allowed to push and merge: Maintainers".
The toolbox sets that to "No one", so every change reaches the main branch through a merge request. Someone loosened it
by hand.
And someone pushed a hand edit of the pipeline file straight to the main branch
That loosening lets someone push a hand edit straight to the main branch. GitLab's page for the commit "chore: tweak the
pipeline by hand": one changed file, .gitlab-ci.yml, with one green line added at its end, "# a hand-edited line the
toolbox never wrote".

text.tspan: git commit -am "chore: tweak the pipeline by hand" && git push origin main

g.text: When the developer reloads the framework, both automation tokens are revoked and replaced by
new ones
The developer runs `task devsecops:reload`. It re-applies the project's own answers to the framework files, then redoes
the GitLab setup. On the access-tokens page both tokens are active, and both install-day tokens sit under "Inactive
project access tokens", marked "Revoked".
The reload replaced them even though they still worked. `task devsecops:init` never does that, as chapter 1 showed.
Then the main branch is locked down again
The same "Protected branches" settings as before the reload. The main branch says "Allowed to push and merge: No one"
again, and "Allowed to merge: Maintainers": a change now reaches the main branch only through a merge request.
And the developer sends the restored pipeline file back through a merge request
The reload also put .gitlab-ci.yml back on disk, without the hand-written line. The main branch is locked, so the
developer commits it on a branch and opens a merge request with the push.
GitLab's page for that commit, the same kind of page as the hand edit: "1 merge request", one changed file,
.gitlab-ci.yml, and the red line "# a hand-edited line the toolbox never wrote" removed.

text.tspan: git switch -c reload-framework && git commit -am "chore: put the framework files back" && git push -o
